title: Adaptive Concept Discovery for Interpretable Few-Shot Text Classification
claim: A concept library is generated by an LLM, used for two-stage similarity prediction, and refined from misclassified samples.
layout: 3 regions, left-to-right with feedback loop, shaded panels, LLM diamonds
description: A wide pipeline diagram split into three hatched regions. On the left, Concept Generation: class nodes y1, y2, y3 (blue circles) feed green diamonds (LLM) that output yellow prototypical concept boxes C_p and orange discriminative pair boxes C_d^{i,j}. These connect to blue database cylinders X1–X3, then to a tall purple Annotation and Selection bar. A hollow arrow leads to the upper right Two-stage Prediction panel. A test-sample cylinder feeds pink similarity score boxes s_p, top-k selection in a gray box, and discriminative scores s_d. These are blended with weights α and 1−α into s^1(x), s^2(x) and a purple Prediction box. At bottom right, Concept Tuning takes a misclassified sample and related concepts into Semantic and Logical Tuning boxes. Feedback arrows loop back to Annotation and Selection. Pastel colors encode the module types.
caption: The framework of StructCBM. We first prompt an LLM to generate an initial library of prototypical concepts Cp and discriminative concepts Cd. Next, we predict with the concept library in a two-stage process: we first select candidate labels by ranking sample similarities with Cp, and then finalize the label through a contrastive comparison among these candidates using Cd. For misclassified samples, we semantically or logically refine the concept library based on their feedback in the concept tuning stage.
abstract: Few-shot text classification is a critical real-world task for which Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown great promise. However, their high inference costs and lack of interpretability limit their practical use. While Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) offer an efficient and interpretable alternative, their reliance on training surrogate models makes them incompatible with few-shot scenarios. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel CBM paradigm that relies solely on sample-concept similarity to make predictions. We ensure the effectiveness of our concepts through a prototypical-discriminative dual-level architecture and a dynamic concept refinement mechanism. Extensive experiments show that with as few as 10 training samples, our method surpasses prior CBMs and even achieves performance comparable to LLMs. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/alexiszlf/StructCBM}.
